items.title: Switching doors doubles your chance of the car
items.claim: Three doors, one car, two goats. Pick a door. Monty (who knows where the car is) opens a different door revealing a goat. Should you switch?
items.prompt: What's the probability of winning if you switch?

options.text: 1/3 — first guess was 1/3, opening a door doesn't change anything
2/3 — your first guess had 1/3 chance of being right, so the remaining unopened door now carries the original 2/3 probability of the OTHER two doors combined
100 percent — Monty's reveal guarantees the win

items.reveal_title: Marilyn vos Savant and a thousand wrong PhDs
items.reveal:
Vos Savant published the answer 'switch' in Parade magazine in 1990. Thousands of readers wrote in — including PhDs in mathematics — insisting she was wrong. She was right.

The key: Monty knows where the car is and always reveals a goat. Your initial choice has 1/3 probability of the car. The OTHER two doors together have 2/3 probability. Monty's reveal removes one of those two doors but doesn't change the 2/3 — it now sits entirely on the remaining unopened door.

If Monty acted randomly (sometimes revealing the car himself), switching wouldn't help — but he doesn't. His knowledge is essential.

The Monty Hall puzzle is the canonical demonstration that conditional probability defeats intuition. Run the simulation 1000 times: switching wins about 667 of them, sticking wins 333.
items.why: Probability intuition assumes 'two outcomes equally likely'. Conditional probability — conditioning on what Monty reveals — distinguishes outcomes that 'look' symmetric but aren't.

items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.

items.title: A skydiver and a feather hit terminal velocity at hugely different speeds — but the math is the same
items.claim: Drop a steel ball: terminal velocity ~150 m/s. Drop a person: ~50 m/s. Drop a feather: ~1 m/s. All fall under the same gravity. The differences come from one equation: weight equals drag.

options.text: Terminal velocity is where gravitational force (mg, downward) exactly balances drag force (proportional to v squared for high speeds, or v for low speeds); the equilibrium speed depends on mass, cross-sectional area, drag coefficient and air density
Only on the height of the fall
Drag is the same for all objects

items.reveal_title: The drag equation and limit velocities
items.reveal:
For an object falling through air, two forces:
- Gravity: mg, downward.
- Drag: at high speed, F_drag = (1/2) * rho * v^2 * C_d * A, where rho is air density, C_d is drag coefficient, A is cross-sectional area.

At terminal velocity, drag equals gravity: v_terminal = sqrt(2 * m * g / (rho * C_d * A)).

Approximate terminal velocities:
- Steel ball (cm-scale): ~150 m/s.
- Skydiver in spread-eagle: ~50 m/s.
- Skydiver in head-first dive: ~90 m/s.
- Tennis ball: ~30 m/s.
- Raindrop (1mm): ~6.5 m/s.
- Snowflake: ~0.5-1 m/s.
- Dust mote: micrometres per second.

The famous 'Galileo dropped balls from the leaning tower of Pisa' demonstrates that g is the same for all masses — but only in vacuum. In air, lighter objects with high surface area to mass ratio fall slower because of drag.

Apollo 15 (1971): astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the lunar surface (no atmosphere). They hit the ground simultaneously — Galileo confirmed live on Earth television.

Felix Baumgartner (Red Bull Stratos jump, 2012) reached supersonic terminal velocity (~377 m/s) by jumping from the stratosphere where air is thinner. He broke the sound barrier with his body.
items.why: Galileo showed all objects fall the same — in vacuum. In air, drag dominates within seconds and terminal velocity is set by an unfamiliar combination of properties. The intuition only holds in idealised conditions.
